approachQuestion.prompt:
Nearest Exit. A rooted binary tree models rooms reachable through child doors. A room with no children is an exit. Return the smallest number of doors from the root to an exit. A root that is already an exit returns 0.

In examples, x(left,right) denotes a node labelled x, and - denotes an absent child. Example 1: Input: 1(2(3(-,-),-),4(-,-)). Output: 1. Example 2: Input: 9(-,8(-,7(-,-))). Output: 2. Example 3: Input: 6(-,-). Output: 0.

Constraints: 1 <= n <= 200000; the immutable tree has child pointers only, no cycles or shared nodes. Shape is unrestricted. A missing child is not a room or an exit. All doors have equal cost. Either breadth-first or full depth-first examination is acceptable.

options.text: Process (node,distance) pairs in a FIFO queue from the root. Return the distance of the first dequeued node having no children.
options.feedback: The queue removes nodes in increasing distance, so the first actual leaf has minimum distance.

options.text: Visit all nodes with a depth-first stack carrying their root distances, updating a minimum only at leaves. Return that minimum.
options.feedback: Every actual exit is considered, so visiting order cannot corrupt the minimum. Its height-dependent storage differs from the queue.

options.text: Visit all nodes, store the distance of every leaf, sort all stored distances, and return the first.
options.feedback: All leaf distances are correct, but sorting is unnecessary; a running minimum or first breadth-first leaf gives the answer.

options.text: Use left-first depth-first search and return immediately upon reaching its first leaf.
options.feedback: In Example 1 the left leaf is 2 doors away, but the right leaf is only 1 door away.

feedback.reason: A nearest leaf requires minimum complete root-to-leaf distance, not the first leaf in an arbitrary depth-first order.
details: Enqueue the root with distance zero. Repeatedly dequeue one room. If it has no children, return its distance; otherwise enqueue each existing child with distance plus one. Never enqueue missing children.

A leaf has no existing children; a null child is not itself an exit. Breadth-first order reaches the smallest edge distance first. Depth-first first-leaf search would depend on branch order rather than nearest distance.

“Process (node,distance) pairs in a FIFO queue from the root. Return the distance of the first dequeued node having no children.”: The queue removes nodes in increasing distance, so the first actual leaf has minimum distance.

“Visit all nodes with a depth-first stack carrying their root distances, updating a minimum only at leaves. Return that minimum.”: Every actual exit is considered, so visiting order cannot corrupt the minimum. Its height-dependent storage differs from the queue.

“Visit all nodes, store the distance of every leaf, sort all stored distances, and return the first.”: All leaf distances are correct, but sorting is unnecessary; a running minimum or first breadth-first leaf gives the answer.
“Use left-first depth-first search and return immediately upon reaching its first leaf.”: In Example 1 the left leaf is 2 doors away, but the right leaf is only 1 door away.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed FIFO method. Let n be the node count, h the height in nodes, and w the largest number of nodes at one depth. What is the tight worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair? Count queue entries and scalar state; exclude the input and scalar result. Queue insertion/removal takes constant time and removes processed entries rather than retaining a full history.
constraints: All legal shapes are allowed; do not assume balance. Heights count nodes, not edges.

Pointer access, comparisons, arithmetic on the stated integer ranges, and allocation/release of a fixed-size frame take constant time. No hashing is used. Count all live explicit frames; the method does not use language recursion or copy paths/subtrees unless explicitly stated.

feedback.reason: A breadth-first frontier may require linear node visits and width-sized storage.
details: Each node enters and leaves the queue at most once. Before finding a leaf, a wide complete tree can require linear work and a full frontier; the queue spans at most two adjacent levels, hence O(w).
FIFO order processes all smaller distances before larger ones. A node qualifies only when both children are absent, so no missing-child shortcut can produce a false exit.

“O(n) time, O(w) auxiliary space”: Each node enters and leaves the queue at most once. Before finding a leaf, a wide complete tree can require linear work and a full frontier; the queue spans at most two adjacent levels, hence O(w).
“O(n) time, O(h) auxiliary space”: Height controls a depth-first stack, not a breadth-first queue. Wide shallow trees separate these bounds.
“O(h) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Many nodes can precede the nearest leaf in queue order, and the queue may be wide.
“O(n) time, O(nh) auxiliary space”: Distances are scalar fields; complete paths are not stored. The queue is bounded by adjacent level widths.
